title: 📘 UNIT 2: AFRICA AND THE COLONIAL EXPERIENCE (1880s–1960s)
notes:
Colonialism → political, economic and social control of one country or territory by another.

The late 19th century saw rapid European expansion and the partition of Africa.

 African societies responded through peaceful and armed resistance, while colonial powers established different systems of administration and economic exploitation.

title: 2.1 💱 The Era of “Legitimate Trade” and Colonial Empires
notes:
“Legitimate Trade” → trade in African commodities that replaced the Trans-Atlantic slave trade.

Major exports included:
• Gum.
• Groundnuts.
• Palm products, especially palm oil.

European manufactured imports included cloth, alcoholic drinks and firearms.

📌 The new trade benefited mainly rulers, wealthy merchants and European traders, while indigenous industries and living conditions of many Africans remained weak.

title: 2.1.1 🚢 From Slave Trade to Legitimate Trade
notes:
Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade → “Illegitimate Trade” because human beings were traded as commodities.

Abolition movements and the Industrial Revolution weakened and eventually ended the slave trade.

European industries increasingly demanded:
• Raw materials.
• Food supplies.
• New markets for manufactured goods.

This helped shift European interest toward direct economic and territorial control in Africa.

title: 2.1.2 🏭 Infrastructure and Ideology of New Imperialism
notes:
New Imperialism → intensified European expansion from the second half of the 19th century to the outbreak of World War I.

Technological advantages included:
• Better firearms.
• Steamships and river boats.
• Improved transportation.
• Improved communication.
• Medical advances against tropical diseases.

Economic factors → raw materials, markets, investment opportunities and food supplies.

Political factors → national prestige, strategic interests and rivalry among European powers.

Ideological factors → nationalism, missionary activity and ideas used to justify European domination.

title: 2.1.3 🗺️ Partition of Africa
notes:
Scramble for Africa → rapid European competition to acquire African territories, especially during the 1880s and 1890s.

Major motives:
• Search for raw materials.
• Search for markets.
• Investment opportunities.
• Strategic interests.
• National prestige.
• Competition among European powers.
• Missionary and ideological motives.

title: 2.1.4 🤝 Berlin Conference (1884–1885)
notes:
Berlin Conference → European meeting concerning the partition and occupation of Africa.

• Held in Berlin under Otto von Bismarck.
• African countries were not represented.
• European powers established rules for claiming African territories.
• European powers agreed on free trade in the Congo Basin and free navigation on the Niger River.
• “Effective occupation” became important for maintaining territorial claims.

📌 The conference accelerated the European partition of Africa.

title: 2.2 🛡️ African Resistance against Colonial Expansion
notes:
African resistance occurred throughout areas of European expansion.

Methods included:
• Peaceful resistance.
• Armed resistance.
• Refusal to accept foreign control.
• Defense of political sovereignty and independence.

European colonizers often used unequal treaties, military force and superior weapons to establish colonial rule.

📌 African resistance was based strongly on the defense of sovereignty.

title: 2.2.1 ⚔️ Samori Toure of Mandinka
notes:
Samori Toure → Muslim military and political leader who established the Wassoulou Empire in West Africa.

• Built a strong and organized army.
• Acquired modern firearms.
• Resisted French expansion.
• Used military organization and strategic resistance against French forces.
• French forces eventually defeated him after prolonged conflict.

📌 Samori Toure became one of the major symbols of West African resistance to French colonial expansion.

title: 2.2.2 🇪🇬 Urabi Pasha's Resistance
notes:
Urabi Pasha → Egyptian military and nationalist leader who opposed foreign influence and control in Egypt.

His movement challenged the political dominance of the Khedive and increasing European influence.

British military intervention eventually defeated the movement, strengthening British control over Egypt.

title: 2.2.3 🌙 The Mahdist Movement in Sudan
notes:
Mahdist Movement → Islamic religious and political movement against Egyptian-Ottoman and British influence in Sudan.

Muhammad Ahmad → proclaimed himself the Mahdi and led the movement.

Major developments:
• Mahdist forces defeated Egyptian forces.
• Khartoum was captured in 1885.
• General Charles Gordon was killed.
• Khalifa Abdullah succeeded the Mahdi after his death.
• Anglo-Egyptian forces defeated the Mahdists at Omdurman in 1898.
• Sudan was placed under an Anglo-Egyptian Condominium.

title: 2.2.4 🌿 Maji-Maji Rebellion
notes:
Maji-Maji Rebellion → major anti-German resistance in Tanganyika, beginning in 1905.

Causes:
• Heavy taxation.
• Forced labor.
• Forced cotton production.
• Colonial exploitation.

Maji-Maji → sacred water believed by participants to protect them from German bullets.

Results:
• German military suppression.
• Scorched-earth tactics.
• Destruction of villages and crops.
• Famine and loss of life.
• Destruction of trade and wealth.

📌 The rebellion encouraged later African nationalism.

title: 2.2.5 💪 Strengths and Weaknesses of African Resistance
notes:
Strengths:
• Strong defense of sovereignty.
• Courage and determination.
• Knowledge of local environments.
• Religious and cultural motivation.
• Formation of temporary alliances.

Weaknesses:
• Lack of unity among African societies.
• Rivalries between states and groups.
• Inferior weapons and military technology.
• Limited coordination and communication.
• European military superiority.

📌 Resistance differed in intensity and organization from one region to another.

title: 2.3 🏛️ Colonial Administration and the Colonial States
notes:
European colonial powers established political systems to control African territories and populations.

Major colonial policies:
• British → Indirect Rule.
• French → Direct Rule / Assimilation.

Colonial administration controlled political authority while colonial economies focused on agriculture, mining, trade and the extraction of African resources.

title: 2.3.1 🇬🇧 British Colonial Policy — Indirect Rule
notes:
Indirect Rule → administration through existing African rulers and institutions under British supervision.

Frederick Lugard → major developer of British Indirect Rule.

Features:
• Used local chiefs and traditional authorities.
• Required fewer European officials.
• Maintained selected traditional institutions under colonial control.
• Often emphasized differences between communities.
• Applied the principle of “divide and rule.”

📌 Indirect Rule was considered relatively inexpensive and practical for governing large territories.

title: 2.3.2 🇫🇷 French Colonial Policy — Direct Rule
notes:
Direct Rule → stronger administrative control by French colonial authorities.

Assimilation → attempt to make selected colonial subjects adopt French language, laws, culture and political practices.

Albert Sarraut → associated with the development of French Direct Rule.

📌 French policy generally aimed at closer integration of colonies into the French system than British Indirect Rule.

title: 2.3.3 🌾 Colonial Agriculture
notes:
Colonial agricultural policies focused heavily on producing cash crops for export.

Effects:
• Expansion of cash-crop production.
• Colonial taxation pushed peasants toward cash crops.
• Food-crop production was sometimes neglected.
• African farmers became dependent on imported manufactured goods.
• Low prices for African products and high prices for imports reduced peasant incomes.
• Soil exhaustion and famine occurred in some areas.

title: 2.3.4 ⛏️ Colonial Mining
notes:
Mining was one of the most profitable areas for European investment.

Major resources:
• Gold.
• Copper.
• Coal.
• Asbestos.
• Tin.

Important mining regions:
• Katanga → copper.
• Northern Rhodesia/Zambia → copper belt.
• Southern Rhodesia → gold, copper and asbestos.
• Witwatersrand → major mining center in southern Africa.

📌 Colonial authorities controlled mineral resources and leased them mainly to European companies.

title: 2.3.5 🚂 Colonial Transport and Infrastructure
notes:
Colonial governments built:
• Railways.
• Roads.
• Ports.
• Communication facilities.

The main purpose was to transport raw materials from production areas to ports for export rather than to create integrated African economies.

📌 Infrastructure primarily served colonial economic and administrative interests.

title: 2.3.6 👥 Social and Political Effects of Colonialism
notes:
Social effects:
• Growth of towns and urbanization.
• Rural-to-urban migration.
• Emergence of new social classes.
• Changes in education, religion and culture.
• Disruption of traditional lifestyles.

Political effects:
• Loss of African sovereignty.
• Imposition of foreign political systems.
• Creation and restructuring of colonial states.
• Division among communities.
• Development of African nationalist movements.

title: 2.3.7 💰 Economic Effects of Colonialism
notes:
• African economies became oriented toward European needs.

• Raw materials were exported to Europe.

• European manufactured goods entered African markets.

• Indigenous industries were weakened.

• Colonial taxation increased pressure on Africans.

• Profits and resources were largely controlled by colonial powers.

• Transport systems mainly connected resource-producing areas with ports.

• Economic dependence continued after political independence in many African states.

title: 2.3.8 🏺 Cultural Effects of Colonialism
notes:
• European languages and cultural practices spread.

• Indigenous cultural practices were weakened in many areas.

• Christian missionary activity expanded.

• Traditional religious beliefs were challenged.

• European names, education and lifestyles were introduced.

• Some African cultural institutions survived and adapted under colonial conditions.

title: 🏆 UNIT 2 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
💱 Legitimate Trade → replaced slave trade → gum, groundnuts, palm oil and other commodities.

🏭 New Imperialism → capitalism + technology + raw materials + markets + political rivalry.

🗺️ Berlin Conference → 1884–1885 → European rules for partitioning Africa; Africans were not represented.

🛡️ African Resistance:
Samori Toure → West Africa → French expansion.
Urabi Pasha → Egypt → foreign influence.
Mahdist Movement → Sudan → Muhammad Ahmad → Omdurman, 1898.
Maji-Maji → Tanganyika → German colonial rule, 1905–1907.

🏛️ Colonial Administration:
Britain → Indirect Rule → Frederick Lugard.
France → Direct Rule / Assimilation → Albert Sarraut.

🌾 Colonial economy → cash crops + mining + raw-material exports + foreign markets.

📌 Main colonial effects → political domination, economic exploitation, social change, cultural disruption and long-term economic dependence.

🧠 EXAM TIP:
Remember the contrast:
British → Indirect Rule → local authorities.
French → Direct Rule → stronger central colonial control.
